papers.title: QWeaver: Quantum Circuit Cut Workflow with MLIR-based Compiler, Runtime, and Weaver Hybrid Tasks
papers.abstract: Quantum computers available today are constrained by limited qubit counts and high noise levels, making the direct execution of large quantum circuits infeasible on a single device, and while quantum circuit cutting addresses this by partitioning a large circuit into smaller subcircuits for independent execution, orchestrating the full end-to-end workflow remains a significant programming challenge. In this paper, we present QWeaver, a task-graph-based programming and orchestration workflow framework for quantum circuit cutting that accepts OpenQASM quantum circuits as input and constructs a directed acyclic task graph. In this graph, the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR)-based circuit cut is the first task, responsible for analyzing and partitioning the input circuit into executable fragment representations; the generated fragments are then handed to a set of quantum circuit execution tasks that depend on the cut task and can be dispatched concurrently across available quantum backends via the Quantum Intelligent Runtime System (Q-IRIS). Finally, a weaving task, dependent on all execution tasks, performs classical post-processing that applies quasi-probability reconstruction techniques to combine the sampled measurement outcomes of all fragments and recover an accurate approximation of the original circuit's output distribution. We describe the architecture of QWeaver, its integration with Q-IRIS and the execution engine for the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR-EE), validate end-to-end reconstruction on GHZ and Harris-Ross instances, and evaluate systems and width trade-offs on structured GHZ simulator workloads.

papers.title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

papers.title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup. Recent machine learning--based cofolding models have reported accuracy approaching that of FEP---and at least one of them, Boltz-2, has already been widely adopted for affinity prediction---but they remain expensive for large computational screens and even more expensive for retraining on newly collected experimental data. To address these challenges, we introduce STORM: Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules. STORM is a fast, simple machine learning model that ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and molecule representations for binding affinity prediction. Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds the accuracy of Boltz-2 on multiple evaluation datasets, while delivering a speed improvement of over five orders of magnitude for both inference and training. Our results also suggest opportunities to substantially improve affinity prediction accuracy by integrating historical experimental affinity data with structural and biophysical information.

papers.title: Physics-Guided Crystal Structure Elucidation from Powder X-Ray Diffraction with Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Determining unique atomic coordinates from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) remains challenging because peak overlap, weak scattering from light elements, limited scattering contrast between elements with similar atomic numbers, and experimental noise render the inverse problem underdetermined. Here, we present XCAPE (XRD-Constrained Accelerated Prediction Engine), a crystal structure prediction (CSP) framework that integrates experimentally derived composition, unit cell parameters, space group, and PXRD data into a symmetry-aware evolutionary search. XCAPE explores Wyckoff-site configurations using tailored mutation operations, evaluates candidates by both energetic stability and diffraction agreement, and accelerates geometry optimization using a universal machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP). The framework recovered 71 of 77 database-derived benchmark structures (92.2%) from simulated PXRD patterns and all 12 reference structures from experimental PXRD patterns. It further identified 12 candidate structure assignments that are consistent with experimental PXRD patterns, lack matching entries in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD), and are thermodynamically competitive at the MLIP level. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations showed that 10 of these 12 candidates lie within 10 meV/atom of the convex hull. By bridging experimental diffraction data and physically plausible atomistic models, XCAPE can provide structural insight into previously unresolved materials and support accelerated materials discovery in automated research workflows.

papers.title: Toward Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Neural AC Power Flow
papers.abstract: Growing uncertainty in power system operations from renewables integration, extreme weather, and data center loads challenges the reliability of traditional power flow solvers at scale. Machine learning-based proxies are a potentially promising alternative, but the prohibitive cost of generating training data for large grids makes out-of-distribution generalization a key capability for deployment; currently, models trained on small grids lack that capability. In this work, we systematically evaluate how physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, and perturbation-based data augmentation improve the zero-shot transfer of three graph neural network-based power flow models from smaller systems to a larger, unseen 500-bus system. We find that (1) physics-informed losses improve transfer relative to purely supervised objectives; (2) multi-grid training on smaller systems matches the best single grid but does not close the gap to target-grid training; (3) perturbation-based augmentation on edge attributes improves transfer by up to 54.6%; and (4) random line/generator dropout does not consistently improve performance.

papers.title: When Price Charts Rhyme: Historical Visual Retrieval for Stock Return Prediction
papers.abstract: We study whether visually similar price histories predict similar future returns, using a vision model to retrieve each stock's most similar charts from three decades of U.S. price histories. A representation pretrained only on natural images already retrieves neighbors whose realized returns predict the cross-section of stock returns. Aligning the representation with subsequent returns more than doubles the strategy's Sharpe ratio and outperforms a convolutional neural network trained directly on chart images. The predictability is concentrated among stocks with greater limits to arbitrage. Returns and order imbalances around portfolio formation indicate that the signal identifies temporary selling pressure that partially reverts. A sparse autoencoder traces the return-aligned signal to recurring visual states that determine which historical charts are retrieved. Our approach traces each forecast to dated historical charts, making it more transparent than direct image-to-return models and linking rule-based technical analysis with machine-learning chart reading.

papers.title: FlowSH: Detecting Web Attacks by Correlating Anomalous Network Flows and Endpoint Logs
papers.abstract: Web applications compose the core of internet services, rendering them prominent targets for audacious attackers. Among web attacks, SQL injection (SQLi) remains a persistent, damaging web applications connected to databases. The widespread adoption of HTTPS has been a critical advancement for online security, ensuring the confidentiality and integrity of communications by encrypting network payloads. However, it also renders traditional Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) less effective, as these typically rely on packet inspection of plaintext traffic. To access encrypted payloads, some NIDS resort to TLS-interception proxies, which leads to data leaks and security risks. This paper presents FlowSH, a system for detecting web attacks that is agnostic to whether the traffic is encrypted (HTTPS) or not (HTTP). Rather than decrypting packets in transit, FlowSH correlates flow-level metadata (NetFlows) with endpoint logs, which inherently contain decrypted payloads after reaching the web server. The system combines unsupervised machine learning to flag anomalous NetFlows and similarity search over server-side logs using Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to confirm attacks. We implemented and evaluated FlowSH in a testbed with multiple web scanners and demonstrated its detection effectiveness, detecting 70% of SQLi attacks missed by ModSecurity, a leading web application firewall.

papers.title: Protecting Web Applications using a Multimodal AI-based System for Classifying Web Injection Attacks
papers.abstract: Web applications have been essential to accessing and managing online services. Made available with weaknesses, much due to their rapid development and human error, they are exposed to frequent web injection attacks, leaving security analysts overwhelmed with threats and alerts that often lack critical details for proper risk assessment. Detecting these attacks requires inspecting the payload of network traffic packets, which becomes inaccessible when traffic is encrypted via HTTPS, as encryption hides the content of the traffic. This paper introduces a Multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI) system to protect online services that rely on web application security by detecting and classifying web injection attacks, and provides security analysts with information to support attack prevention and incident response. The system employs unsupervised Machine Learning (ML) to flag potentially anomalous Network Flows (NetFlows). The corresponding data recorded in Web Server Logs (WebLogs) is then analysed using a heuristic framework based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) and supervised ML to detect and classify web injection attacks. Finally, the resulting classifications are scrutinised using a Similarity Search Engine (SSE) based on Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to validate them. The solution handles encrypted traffic by analysing NetFlows and WebLogs, the latter in their natural, unencrypted form, by leveraging NetFlow-level metadata for anomaly detection and analysing web server logs after TLS termination, thereby avoiding any additional in-network traffic decryption. It was evaluated in the classification of eight web injection attack classes. The results demonstrated its ability to accurately identify attacks and their classes, achieving an F_1 score of 91% and an accuracy of 95%, and offering valuable insights for alert prioritisation.

papers.title: Time-Varying Bayesian Optimization and Extremum Seekingfor Drift-Tube Linac Tuning at LANSCE
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) has emerged as a promising machine learning approach to accelerator tuning. It has the advantage of being able to incorporate prior information, including simulation and historical data, and explicitly model measurement noise. However, standard implementations can produce large, abrupt parameter updates that are undesirable and potentially unsafe in accelerator operation. They may also spend excessive time exploring less promising regions of the search space. We address these limitations by imposing soft and hard step size limits. We evaluate these methods by adjusting the radio frequency settings of the drift tube linac (DTL) at the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE) to maximize the particle count at the end of the linac. We first test the methods in simulation with constant exogenous parameters, then repeat the tests with drifting exogenous parameters. Under drifting conditions, progressively reducing the BO step size limit improved convergence. We also find that an initial BO segment followed by extremum seeking (ES), an approach we call BO-ES, combines BO's use of prior information and sample efficiency with ES's effectiveness in local optimization and drift tracking. Finally, tests on the LANSCE accelerator with BO-ES demonstrate an approximately $25\%$ reduction in losses at the end of the linac across different configurations of historical and simulation data.

papers.title: Optical Neural Networks Should Be Evaluated by Function, Not Only Physics
papers.abstract: Optical neural networks (ONNs) are attracting significant attention as alternative platforms for machine learning (ML). In an ONN, an optical module often takes over part of the computation inside a digital ML pipeline. How much of the task does the optical module itself perform, and how much does it contribute to any claimed system-level advantages, such as throughput or energy?   This paper offers a simple, function-oriented evaluation methodology. Whatever its internal physics, the optical module appears to the surrounding digital pipeline as a mapping between real-valued tensors. We therefore evaluate it in three steps: (i) define its boundary in the pipeline, as real-valued tensors in and out; (ii) replace it with standard digital modules to identify those that match the optical system's performance on the same task and metric; and (iii) state system-level claims, such as speed or energy, per inference against the performance-matched digital module. We summarize steps (i) and (ii) in an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its use on published ONN systems. This helps isolate the optical module's contribution and provides a concrete digital reference for assessing its claimed system-level advantages, without the need to understand the physics.   While we focus on optical systems as the most prominent example, the same approach applies to any physical analog computing platform used in ML, wherever a physical module takes over part of a digital pipeline.

papers.title: Machine-learned acceleration of earthquake sequence simulations
papers.abstract: Earthquake sequence simulations involve slow interseismic processes and rapid dynamic ruptures. During interseismic periods, a numerical solver can take large time steps efficiently. During seismic periods, in contrast, the solver must drastically reduce the time step, and elastodynamic wave-mediated memory effects become significant; long-term simulations are therefore computationally expensive. We investigate the use of neural operators to accelerate earthquake sequence simulations. We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) on data from high-fidelity, fully dynamic simulations to learn a jump map that advances the system state from before a seismic rupture to after it. We propose a hybrid modeling framework in which a conventional quasi-dynamic solver simulates the slow interseismic evolution, and the trained FNO replaces the solver during the computationally intensive seismic periods with wave-mediated inertial effects. The hybrid model reproduces key long-term statistics of fully dynamic simulations, including distributions of event magnitudes and recurrence times. Furthermore, it provides a much better approximation to the fully dynamic simulations than the commonly used quasi-dynamic approximation at a reduced computational expense.

papers.title: Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite Qubit System
papers.abstract: Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.

papers.title: Application of Pretrained Universal Machine Learning Force-Fields for Phase Transitions Prediction in ZrO2
papers.abstract: Pretrained universal machine-learning force fields can reduce the cost of finite-temperature molecular dynamics relative to density functional theory. However, most benchmarks test only static properties and do not assess whether these models reproduce the correct phase-transition sequence. Here, we benchmark ten open-source universal machine-learning force fields for zirconia (ZrO$_2$) using phonon dispersion calculations and variable-cell isothermal-isobaric molecular dynamics. Zirconia is a useful test because it has three thermodynamically stable crystalline phases prior to melting, following the sequence monoclinic-tetragonal-cubic. Four models reproduce this sequence: 7net-l3i5, MatterSim-v1.0.0-1M, MACE-mpa, and MACE-D3. Models with orthorhombic-tetragonal energy errors above about 10 meV/atom (7net-0, CHGNet, and MACE) instead produce an orthorhombic intermediate and predict monoclinic-orthorhombic-tetragonal-cubic-liquid upon heating. ORB-based models fail to sustain stable variable-cell dynamics because their phonon frequencies are compressed by 30-60% relative to the density functional theory reference. Across all ten models, two ground-state diagnostics predict finite-temperature behavior. Relative polymorph energetics should agree with the matched density functional theory reference within about 6 meV/atom, and the phonon spectrum should not show systematic softening. These diagnostics are practical screening metrics for assessing pretrained force fields for phase-transition predictions.

papers.title: From Arraignment to Resolution: Transformer Models of Court Cases
papers.abstract: The criminal legal system is composed of many complex decision points, such as which charges are pursued, how bond is determined, plea deal negotiations, and sentencing. Given the profound impact of such decisions, there is a growing need to increase the transparency within this system. While prior machine learning approaches have focused on modeling single decisions (e.g., recidivism), this paper proposes a transformer-based time series model to forecast the outcome of the next proceeding in a case (e.g., charges accepted, bond set, plea deal made, etc.). By modeling a case as an event sequence, we enable a more nuanced analysis to support better oversight and understanding of decision making. We conduct an empirical analysis of thousands of cases using a newly constructed dataset derived from publicly available court records of a mid-sized U.S. city. We fit models that combine textual data from clerk notes with structured information about the defendant, prior charges, and courtroom. Our transformer model achieves $.57$ micro-F1 on a 20-class multi-label task, a significant improvement over several baselines and comparable to a GRU trained on the same input. We demonstrate how the model can be used to provide insights into decision-making and help court observers identify emerging issues within the jurisdiction studied.

papers.title: Foundation Model-Driven Agentic AI for 6G
papers.abstract: Mobile networks are outgrowing manual tuning: parameters multiply, services diversify, and traffic shifts faster than experts can react. The machine learning (ML) models that automate radio control are narrow: each is trained for one task, degrades when conditions move, and needs specialist retraining. This article introduces FM-in-the-loop, a framework for 6G radio access networks in which a foundation model (FM) reasons while lightweight machine learning agents act. It reads operator intents in plain language, decomposes them into subtasks, coordinates task-specific agents over Model Context Protocol (MCP) interfaces, and supervises them across their lifecycle---while the orchestration FM never enters the latency-critical control path. We locate seven integration points across four lifecycle stages, compare three cloud-to-edge deployments, and evaluate two elements: channel representations from a wireless FM are tested under noise-level and channel-estimation-error shift, and an instrumented emulation of the orchestration loop reports the measured cost of turning an operator intent into dispatched agent goals. Hallucination, cost, and standardization barriers remain.

papers.title: AllotNet: an Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Choice Model for Moral Judgement in Humanitarian Aid Allocation, Validated against a Planted Synthetic Population
papers.abstract: Official development assistance fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025, and the decision of who is helped first when there is not enough for everyone is moving into software. A leading published machine-learning targeting system excluded 53 per cent of eligible households as deployed. If the rule of distribution ends up in code, it should carry the judgement of many cultures, and the machine should execute while a person judges. AllotNet is an interpretable mixture-of-experts conditional logit for the allocation judgements elicited by Allot, a pre-registered six-language instrument: eight linear taste experts over seven ethical criteria, weighted by a gate over participant context, with a damped residual, an encoder for household intake, an outcome head and a budget-constrained planner that builds a review queue and never rejects anyone. A model of human judgement has no answer key on real data, so we wrote one first: a planted synthetic population of 5.6 million sessions and 104 million responses (98 million usable choices), generated by the production code path from a ground truth hidden from the loss. All sixteen pre-specified checks passed: criterion ranking $ρ= 1.000$, hidden segments recovered (ARI 0.671), outcome head at 99 per cent of the noise ceiling, planner at 99.4 per cent of oracle. The caveats are reported with them: two checks are weaker than their titles, and a live-generation failure cost 260,712 seeds. The model has 23,550 parameters, is trained quantisation-aware for NVFP4 with its interpretable core in fp32 (welfare-rank parity $ρ= 0.9937$ at W4A16 on the shipped bundle; one parity threshold was relaxed post hoc), and ships as a 125 KB bundle with C11, Java, Rust and Python runtimes. Nothing has been trained on real data yet; at the study's real scale a hierarchical Bayesian mixed logit is the registered comparator.

papers.title: A Graph-Theoretic Framework for Identifying Mathematical Programming Decompositions
papers.abstract: We develop a framework for identifying combinations of complicating variables and/or constraints that can be used to formulate mathematical programming decompositions. A mathematical program is represented by a graph which accounts for the structural and functional relationship between variables and constraints. Graph projections are used to focus on variable- or constraint-based decompositions. A series of coarsening operations is used to generate a reduced graph based on the original or projected graph. On the reduced graph, we use integer programming to identify different combinations of complicating variables and/or constraints. Specifically, variables and constraints are identified as complicating based on their structural role and/or their functionality (contribution to nonlinearity) in the mathematical program. The framework allows us to assess the viability of different decomposition types (variable, constraint, cross) and identify multiple potential decomposition formulations of the same type (e.g. different combinations of complicating variables for Benders decomposition). The systematic nature of our framework facilitates broader studies into the efficacy of different decompositions across a range of problems including energy markets, process design, and machine learning.

papers.title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation for QCCD Co-Design
papers.abstract: Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures enable scalable trapped-ion quantum computing by dynamically shuttling ions between specialized processing and storage zones. A QCCD can be built with many trap sizes and layouts. Comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity and control constraints, and trusting the target code of each compilation. We present a co-design framework built on one Lean-verified compiler. The hardware description and its operating rules are compiler inputs, so a single theorem covers every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves its program's behavior and obeys the hardware rules. Across 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found takes 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. An AI agent that proposes devices based on our compiler's checked results beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. Our verified compiler provably avoids the 11 defects that we report in three previous compilers. It scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.

papers.title: Optimal Joint Bounds for Sparse Ground-State Energy Estimation and Ground-State Preparation
papers.abstract: Ground-state energy estimation (GSEE) and ground-state preparation (GSP) are fundamental problems in quantum computing. Given a Hamiltonian $H$ with $\|H\|\le1$ and a guiding state $|ψ\rangle$ with overlap at least $γ>0$ with the ground space of $H$, the goal in GSEE is to estimate the ground-state energy of $H$ to additive error $δ$ with failure probability at most $\varepsilon$, while in GSP it is to prepare a state with ground-space weight at least $1-\varepsilon$, given a gap lower bound $Δ$. Their costs are measured by quantum query complexity, i.e., the number of oracle calls needed to access $H$. Recent work proved optimal bounds $Θ(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γδ))$ for GSEE and $Θ(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γΔ))$ for GSP in the time-evolution and block-encoding models. However, these models do not directly account for the sparsity of $H$, measured by the maximum number $s$ of nonzero entries in any row or column. In the sparse-access model, oracles instead return the locations and values of these entries. This introduces the additional parameter $s$, and it remained open how query complexity depends jointly on $s$, $γ$, $δ$ or $Δ$, and $\varepsilon$. We resolve this by proving sparse-query lower bounds $Ω(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γδ))$ for GSEE and $Ω(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γΔ))$ for GSP, even for stoquastic Hamiltonians. We also show that these constructions recover the earlier time-evolution and block-encoding lower-bound scalings. We then give matching upper-bound algorithms in the reversible in-place sparse-location model. Thus, we obtain $Θ(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γδ))$ for GSEE and $Θ(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(γΔ))$ for GSP, showing that $\sqrt{s}$ is necessary and sufficient and completing the joint dependence on all problem parameters.

papers.title: Scrambling leads to entanglement cost in NLQC
papers.abstract: In a non-local quantum computation (NLQC), shared entanglement along with a single simultaneous round of quantum communication is used to implement a joint channel. NLQC has many applications, most of which benefit from an understanding of lower bounds on the entanglement needed to implement a given channel as an NLQC. However, the properties of a channel that lead to it having an entanglement cost in NLQC have remained unclear, with most lower bounds only applying to specially constructed examples. Here, we give a new lower bound technique for unitaries based on scrambling: we find that a unitary has zero entanglement cost if and only if it does not scramble. Further, we find that the tripartite mutual information, an entropic object that quantifies the degree of scrambling, provides a quantitative lower bound on entanglement cost in NLQC. This is the first known lower bound on entanglement cost for unitaries in NLQC which is faithful. Our results also relate scrambling and NLQC for the first time. Leveraging the faithful scrambling based bound, we then show that the controllable correlation, an earlier studied quantity, is also a faithful lower bound, resolving an earlier conjecture of Cleve and May.

papers.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

papers.title: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime
papers.abstract: Ensemble prediction of nonlinear dynamics propagates a probability density whose linear transport equation retains the nonlinear drift, but grid-dependent circuit costs leave end-to-end feasibility in early fault-tolerant quantum computing unresolved. We couple polynomial reduced-order models fitted by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to Walsh-synthesized Koopman-von Neumann (KvN) transport and surface-code resource estimation. At fixed model dimension and drift degree, per-step transport rotation counts scale polylogarithmically with cells per reduced coordinate. Balancing model accuracy against circuit costs makes reduced-model polynomial degree a design variable for early fault-tolerant quantum simulation. For a cylinder wake approaching saturation, preparation, propagation and sampling to 1% relative root-mean-square field error against the radial model are estimated to take 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Estimated three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks below one million qubits. IBM hardware experiments demonstrate nonlinear radial KvN transport for this wake, using reference circuits to mitigate noise.

papers.title: Teleportation of Logical Qubits using Lattice Surgery with Superconducting Circuits
papers.abstract: Demonstrating a quantum advantage when solving large-scale computational problems on a quantum computer requires the correction of errors that occur due to limitations in control accuracy and coherence. Using the concept of quantum error correction, fault-tolerant logical qubits can be realized and manipulated with logical single- and two-qubit gates. In this paper, we experimentally analyze fault-tolerant lattice-surgery, which is a key primitive that enables operations between logical qubits realized in the surface-code. Using this primitive, we demonstrate the teleportation of logical states between two distance-three logical qubits realized in a superconducting circuit composed of 41 physical qubits. Throughout this process, we study the step-by-step transfer of logical information from a source to a target logical qubit by characterizing the time evolution of logical observables. We find that repeated execution of stabilizer measurements, after merging two surface-code patches, restores fault tolerance and yields increased fidelity of the teleported state. When optimizing the protocol in terms of gate count and sequence duration, we observe further improvements in fidelity. Our work offers new insights into the optimization of fault-tolerant lattice-surgery operations, while also providing a comprehensive description of the physical device and gate sequences used. We expect the efficient implementation of increasingly complex logical circuits to enhance the performance of future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

papers.title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows.   This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures.   Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence.   Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

papers.title: Performance of Fusion-Based Quantum Computing with Imperfect Photon Indistinguishability
papers.abstract: Fusion-based quantum computation (FBQC) is a promising route to fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, connecting small entangled resource states through linear-optical fusion measurements. While logical encoding can substantially improve resilience to photon loss, whether these benefits extend to other noise remain an open question. In this work, we show that this is not generally the case when accounting for partial photon distinguishability during resource state generation and fusion measurement. We develop hardware-motivated noise models to capture these effects and investigate their impact on fault tolerance in the 6-ring fusion network. We compare unencoded and Shor(2,2)-encoded resource states prepared using all-photonic and emitter-assisted repeat-until-success (RUS) schemes. For the all-photonic construction, encoding reduces the distinguishability threshold from 0.136% to 0.08%. In contrast, the RUS construction tolerates more distinguishability, with comparable unencoded and encoded thresholds (0.256% and 0.271%, respectively). These results expose a fundamental limitation of evaluating logical encodings under idealized resource-state assumptions and demonstrate that resource-state generation can critically determine the fault tolerance of photonic architectures.

papers.title: Pareto-Informed Smart "Predict, then Optimize" for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Problems
papers.abstract: Many real-world planning applications, from logistics, routing to resource allocation, give rise to optimization problems that need to balance multiple, conflicting objectives. While machine learning is often used to predict the unknown parameters or costs of these problems, standard models trained on prediction accuracy can lead to suboptimal plans. Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) addresses this by integrating the downstream optimization task into the training objective. However, existing DFL methods for multi-objective problems rely on simple scalarization, which fails to capture the rich trade-offs of the Pareto Frontier. To address this gap, we propose a Pareto-aware extension to single-objective Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) for multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems. Our loss function leverages the true Pareto Frontier, forming a target decision that aligns with a sampled preference vector, and minimizes regret against this target. Experiments on multi-objective shortest path and multi-objective knapsack problems show that our approach outperforms traditional two-stage Mean Squared Error (MSE) baselines. It also surpasses scalarization-based SPO+ approaches.

papers.title: Integrating market sentiments for stock price prediction: A comparative study of Bi-LSTM and multilayer perceptions
papers.abstract: This study investigates the integration of sentiment analysis with machine learning models to forecast stock price movements using the Nvidia Corporation as a case study. Sentiment scores were derived from Nvidia-related financial news headlines using two sentiment analysis tools: FinBERT, a domain-specific tool, and TextBlob, a general-purpose tool. These scores were integrated into predictive frameworks based on bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) networks and multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) developed alongside historical stock price data. This study assesses the predictive performance over the entire observation period and across distinct market phases: bullish, stagnation, and strong bullish conditions. The findings indicate that sentiment features enhance predictive accuracy in specific contexts, particularly during stagnation phases, with TextBlob demonstrating superior performance to FinBERT in specific scenarios. In addition, Bi-LSTM models exhibit consistently superior performance in capturing temporal dependencies compared to MLPs. However, the impact of sentiment features diminished during strongly directional trends, such as those observed in strong bullish markets. The combination of FinBERT and TextBlob in the same dataset allows for a dual-perspective approach to sentiment analysis, thereby providing new insights into the dynamic relationship between market sentiment and stock price behavior. This research contributes to the existing literature on applying sentiment analysis to financial forecasting by advancing the integration of complementary sentiment tools and phase-specific evaluations.

papers.title: Identifiability of latent variable models with flexible latent distributions
papers.abstract: Latent variable models are popularly used to characterize dependence among many observed variables through underlying latent variables. Recent advances in statistics and machine learning methods have encouraged growing interest in studying latent variable models with flexible latent distributions that capture complex latent structures. This flexibility, however, raises a fundamental question of whether model parameters can be identified when the latent distribution is unknown and must itself be learned. In this paper, we show that exact identifiability fails almost everywhere, in the sense that distinct but arbitrarily close pairs of model parameters and latent distributions can yield exactly the same distribution for the observed variables. Nonetheless, the resulting identification ambiguity is small. In particular, we prove that the identification ambiguity, measured by the diameter of the set of parameters inducing the same marginal distribution, vanishes at a superpolynomial rate of $\exp\{-c(\log p)^2\}$ as the number of observed variables $p$ grows. Building on this result, we show that the failure of exact identifiability need not preclude consistent estimation or valid inference of the model parameters and latent distribution. These results suggest that, when many variables are observed, the identifiability issue is far less of an obstacle to estimation and inference in latent variable models than is commonly expected.

papers.title: Dissecting the GPU Load/Store Unit and Exposing Its Security Risks
papers.abstract: GPUs are the main platform for large-scale machine learning and power the largest supercomputers. Their load/store units (LSUs) often determine kernel performance and have been exploited in prior attacks. Yet what is known about the LSU is only a few isolated mechanisms and parameters, and even a single one has been enough for an attack. In particular, it is still unknown what a load costs, where loads contend, and even whether a warp can starve due to contention. Until each is measured, neither its security risk nor a defense is known. We reverse-engineer how the LSU serves load instructions on recent NVIDIA GPUs with microbenchmarks and analyze the security implications. We give a cycle-accurate latency formula for a global L1 hit or shared memory access from the addresses it touches, whose address-dependent terms are bank conflicts and the L1 tag lookup; we show that loads contend at both, and that when the LSU pipeline is full a warp can starve a warp of a later-launched block. We then show that the LSU's attack surface is far broader than prior attacks revealed: through channels never exploited before, it can leak information, communicate covertly, and degrade colocated workloads. Through either global bank conflicts or tag lookups alone, we recover a full AES-128 key under the threat model of prior GPU AES timing attacks. Under NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS), the bank access and the tag lookup each open a covert channel across processes, whose rate rises with each GPU generation. Also under MPS, this starvation lets one warp slow a colocated cuBLAS matrix multiplication by up to 750x on the A100 and 563x on the H100.

papers.title: PRISM: A Logical-Physical Boundary Compiler for Dual-Rail Qubits
papers.abstract: Quantum computers can encode each logical qubit across multiple physical degrees of freedom so that errors on the physical qubits can be detected or corrected. A compiler must then translate each logical gate into native instructions, and one gate can have several equivalent realizations that interact through different wires. Routing moves those wires, so a realization chosen before routing can force SWAPs that another would avoid, making code expansion and physical routing a phase-ordering problem. PRISM therefore keeps each gate's realizations open across the logical--physical boundary and commits to one only when routing reaches a layout that can execute it. We formalize which physical circuits implement a gate, which respect the fault model, and which the compiler keeps, and define when a gate can execute under a layout. For dual-rail cavity qubits, logical $\mathrm{CR}_z$ has four loss-admissible realizations, one per rail pairing, and its logical availability graph is exactly the simple quotient of the occupied device graph by the rail pairs. Across 25 workloads with 7 to 25 logical qubits on three device graphs, PRISM reduces routing SWAPs by 20.4--30.8\% and physical depth by 8.8--10.1\% relative to a greedy search that fixes each realization before routing. On the grid and hexagonal lattice, the SWAP reductions hold through 32 logical qubits. By shortening routes, PRISM also reduces photon loss on device models and therefore needs 44.3\% fewer attempts per retained shot at 16 logical qubits, as a geometric mean over workloads and device graphs, and it lowers decoded logical error in a three-round Steane memory under skip-gate leakage.

papers.title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra
papers.abstract: This survey explores the use of Machine Learning (ML) in the field of Computer Algebra (CA), both to optimise existing CA algorithms, and to perform symbolic computation directly. Traditional symbolic methods, while mathematically rigorous, often are computationally expensive thus limiting their use in real-world applications. Recent advances have shown that data-driven techniques can address these limitations by guiding heuristic decisions, selecting optimal algorithms, predicting structural properties of algebraic objects, or even making direct symbolic computations.   We take a systematic literature review approach and uncover work in CA applications including cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gröbner basis computation, symbolic integration, and many more. The survey compares the different ML approaches that have been employed for these tasks, ranging from decision trees to transformers. Issues uncovered by the survey include the lack of benchmark datasets for CA, which hinders the comparison of methods and the generalizability of ML models. The survey identifies the potential for explainable AI tools to help develop trust in decisions, and to drive forward CA research itself.

papers.title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
papers.abstract: We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.

papers.title: Countering Anion Inhibition of Laccase Electron Transfer: Electrostatic Design, Charge-Transfer Dynamics on a Superconducting Quantum Processor, and Its Limits
papers.abstract: Hydroxide at neutral-to-alkaline pH and halides inhibit fungal laccases and limit their use in wastewater treatment. From GFN2-xTB cluster models of Trametes versicolor laccase (PDB 1GYC) we build a four-site Hubbard model of the His454-T3A-T3B-His452 junction of the trinuclear copper cluster and execute its charge-transfer dynamics on the Euro-Q-Exa quantum computer (IQM, 8 qubits, Trotterized circuits with Pauli twirling; 726 jobs). The charge-transfer frequency is measured to 3-5 meV, reproducibly over nine days and across changes of the device qubit map: hydroxide raises the charge-transfer energy of the crystal-geometry model by 92.0 +/- 2.2 meV (exact 87) and exceeds fluoride by 10.1 +/- 1.8 meV. A screen of charged probes in three dielectric models identifies Y116E; in the probe model the hardware resolves a reduction of the hydroxide penalty by 74 +/- 7 meV and of the halide penalty by 64 +/- 5 meV, acting on the site-energy gap rather than on the coupling. A real Glu116 (five conformers) with PROPKA protonation states and the coupled Asp456 gives a realistic reduction of 10-30 meV, with the same sign in 28 of 28 model combinations; the direction and ordering are the prediction, rate factors only an illustration. Scanning the on-site repulsion reverses the sign of the hydroxide effect, and a one-electron Hartree model reproduces the reversal: the measured dynamics is effectively single-particle. On a Fermi-Hubbard benchmark the hardware does not resolve electron correlation; it would need a contrast loss below 0.13 percent per CZ gate instead of the measured 0.34-0.54 percent.

papers.title: CULypso: A Clustered Federated Unlearning paradigm for Vehicular Ad-Hoc Networks
papers.abstract: Unlearning has emerged as an essential security and privacy-preserving solution in Machine Learning, enabling networks to support their clients' rights for data erasure, as mandated by data protection regulations. Introducing such a non-trivial task to an edge, highly mobile and time-sensitive vehicular network is an even greater, largely unexplored challenge. This article argues that a hierarchical Federated Unlearning approach could be aptly integrated into vehicular ad-hoc networks (VANETs), leveraging topology and movement to reduce communication, resource and time costs, while effectively forgetting a client's influence on the global model updates. In order to achieve this, we propose CULypso, an approximate, surgical, hierarchical unlearning algorithm tailored for clustered VANETs. Inspired by the nymph in Greek mythology, Calypso, whose name translates to 'she who conceals the knowledge', CULypso, with the capital letters referencing \textbf{C}lustered \textbf{U}n\textbf{L}earning, aims to achieve exactly what its name suggests: conceal, erase or forget in our case, knowledge it contains. Extensive experiments uphold the potency of our paradigm with it performing approximately 65\% better than FedEraser in terms of time, server storage load, and unlearning fidelity while utterly outperforming baseline full retraining.

papers.title: A Quantum Support Vector Regression Framework for Missing Data Imputation in Ship Performance Data
papers.abstract: The Internet of Ships enables vessels to generate vast amounts of data, yet missing values remain a persistent issue. To the best of the authors' knowledge, existing imputation techniques in this domain rely exclusively on classical machine learning. This study investigates quantum support vector regression (QSVR) for imputing missing values in ship performance data. Classical support vector regression and QSVR models based on different quantum feature maps are compared for estimating marine fuel consumption under varying levels of data availability. The case study uses real-world data from a Panamax bulk carrier, covering 37 variables across six categories. Three experiments are conducted: exploratory analysis with three input features, scalability analysis with increasing dimensionality (3 to 18 features), and comparative evaluation under a selected representative configuration. Across all scenarios, both classical and quantum approaches captured the relationship between the inputs and the main-engine fuel-flow rate, maintaining strong imputation performance even under severe data scarcity. ZZFeatureMap_1 achieved the highest average R2 (0.991 in the performance comparison conducted with 60% of the dataset, 90% missing data, and 14 input features, for instance) and the lowest aggregate imputation errors, while the radial basis function kernel was the strongest classical baseline, delivering highly competitive results.

papers.title: Improving Eddy Detection from Wide-Swath Altimetry with Multimodal Data-Driven Models
papers.abstract: Physically-based eddy detection algorithms usually rely on hard-coded thresholds and constraints that make the detected structures sensitive to small variations in the underlying fields. One way to relax such conditions is the use of machine-learning methodologies that transform the full problem into an optimization process. We present a multimodal, multi-task, data-driven eddy detection framework based on a shallow convolutional U-Net, trained to jointly segment eddy structures and reconstruct the co-located spatial sea surface temperature (SST) anomaly using a dynamically-based reconstruction as target. Two model variants are developed: NADIRnet, trained on conventional nadir altimetry, and SWOTnet, trained through a curriculum that incorporates SWOT-enriched maps. Both models achieve high pixel- and structure-wise detection scores against the ground-truth, with most residual disagreement attributable to boundary placement rather than missed or spurious detections. The coupled SST regression task, enforced through boundary-coupling and gradient-matching loss terms, is shown to sharpen and regularise the detected eddy boundaries. Compared to the dynamically-based reference, both models recover a substantially larger and finer eddy population; notably, SWOTnet's higher-resolution training signal transfers to conventional nadir altimetry thanks to the higher-resolution SST channel, detecting more eddies than a nadir-trained model on the same data. The framework further generalises, even without retraining, to altimetry products and processing levels unseen during training, including SWOT L3 wide-swath retrievals and an independent gridded product. Together with its low computational cost, this framework is thus promising for near-real-time operational deployment and further downstream applications.

papers.title: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in Constrained Combinatorial Optimization with U(1)-Symmetric Tensor Trains
papers.abstract: Tensor Train (TT) decomposition has emerged as a powerful tool for mitigating the curse of dimensionality in a variety of machine learning and combinatorial optimization tasks. Recent advances show that TT-based generative models can efficiently represent and explore high-dimensional discrete spaces, even when the cost function structure is unknown. However, incorporating hard linear constraints into TT-based optimization remains challenging, as existing interpolation and sampling approaches often fail when feasible points are rare. In this work, we develop a general TT-based framework for constrained combinatorial optimization built upon U(1)-symmetric tensor networks. Our method introduces an expressibility-enhancement mechanism for constructing sparse symmetric tensors and a graph-based diversity measure that guides sample selection during training. On assignment benchmarks, expressibility enhancement and diversity-aware selection improve mean solution quality over their respective baselines. The assignment-selected diversifying strategy also extends to nonpolynomial Set Partitioning, with larger relative gains observed in the higher-tensor-rank data families. Separate runtime benchmarks show substantial speedups over ConstrainTNet and PROTES on non-degenerate assignment workloads; comparisons with simulated annealing depend on constraint information and computational budget, but, overall, support the practicality of the current implementation.

papers.title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.

papers.title: Modeling of basic physics issues in toroidal pinches and tools for performance control
papers.abstract: Nonlinear modelling has improved significantly in dealing with physics issues encountered in magnetically confined toroidal pinches, such as the Reversed Field Pinch and Tokamak configurations. Here, recent results relevant to the understanding of helical self-organization processes are presented: formation of internal transport barriers, temporary loss of operational point, relaxation-reconnection events, excitation of Alfvèn waves, and a possible fundamental mechanism for ion heating in plasmas. Starting from physics processes in Reversed Field Pinch plasmas, several similarities with Tokamaks are presented. In addition, data analysis tools, machine learning autoencoding techniques, are here trained for the first time on a RFP data analysis case.

papers.title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.

papers.title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
papers.abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

papers.title: Circuit compilation in the quspect quantum SDK: selecting routings after coupling-constrained resynthesis
papers.abstract: quspect is an open-source quantum computing SDK that provides circuit construction, C++ state-vector simulation with adjoint gradients, support for variational and combinatorial-optimization algorithms, Hamiltonian simulation, control-pulse envelopes and backends for several cloud quantum processors. Here we describe and evaluate its circuit compiler. Routing and synthesis interact: inserting a SWAP can change the circuit structure that later optimization exploits. At its highest optimization level, the compiler evaluates a screened set of routing candidates by their cost after coupling-constrained resynthesis. The pipeline combines parity-state A* search for small CNOT-phase regions, heuristic synthesis for larger regions, and numerical three-qubit instantiation with a per-block 10^-9 check. For a fixed phase polynomial, A* certifies the minimum CX count when it reaches a goal within budget. On an evaluation set of 55 circuits from 41 arXiv papers on five topologies, the compiler uses 0.616 times as many two-qubit gates as Qiskit O3 (95% circuit-cluster bootstrap interval 0.555-0.679) at 0.592 times its depth. BQSKit level 2 reaches 0.853 and tket 0.930. On a 17-qubit superconducting processor, the compiled circuits had the fewest CZ gates in all six scenarios of the main run. Ablations assess the contributions within the integrated pipeline.

papers.title: Supercell periodicity biases octahedral tilting and energetics in high-entropy perovskite oxides
papers.abstract: Odd-period supercells such as $3 \times 3 \times 5$ are often used for equimolar five-component compositions in computational studies of high-entropy perovskite oxides (HEPOs). However, such cells are known to constrain octahedral tilting because they cannot accommodate all standard tilt patterns (Glazer tilt systems). How strongly this constraint affects HEPOs, whose octahedra respond to local cation environments, remains unclear. Here we show that supercell periodicity systematically biases computed octahedral tilting and energetics. Using a machine-learning interatomic potential, we compared odd-period and tilt-commensurate cells for 13 HEPOs. Odd-period cells yielded smaller and less coherent tilts and higher energies, even after configurational averaging. In ~1,700-atom cells, tilt differences persisted in all compositions and energy differences in most. The bias extended to defects, with lower oxygen vacancy formation energies in odd-period cells for strongly tilted compositions. Based on these findings, a simple design rule for equimolar supercells is proposed to lift this constraint.

papers.title: Neural Network Path Optimization for Finding Transition States on a Machine Learned Potential
papers.abstract: Transition states govern chemical reaction rates and outcomes, yet locating them remains a central challenge in computational chemistry. Double-ended search methods find transition states given reactant and product structures, but generally rely on discretized path representations developed for density functional theory, where potential energy surface evaluations are expensive. Machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) dramatically reduce this cost and leverage automatic differentiation to access higher-order derivatives efficiently. We introduce Popcornn, a framework to find transition states by optimizing continuous neural network paths atop an MLIP with a parallelized adaptive numerical integrator. This combination eliminates path discretization artifacts, reduces hyperparameter sensitivity, and enables non-local optimization to overcome local features using second-order potential-energy-surface information. Popcornn consistently recovers more correct transition states than standard methods such as nudged elastic band and growing string, across MLIPs on thousands of organic reactions, establishing it as a robust, automation-ready method for high-throughput transition state search. Popcornn's infrastructure is flexible in path objective, integration strategy, and optimization algorithm, making it a practical tool and platform for investigating open questions in MLIP-based path optimization.

papers.title: Demonstration of a Qubit Control Scheme Compatible with Superconducting Digital Signals
papers.abstract: Superconducting quantum computing faces a critical scalability bottleneck arising from the escalating complexity of traditional analog control infrastructure. Single-Flux-Quantum(SFQ) systems operate at cryogenic temperatures and offer a potential route to addressing these challenges. Using microwave signals at qubit-dependent frequencies to trigger SFQ pulses requires many independent analog microwave sources, limiting the potential to reduce control wiring and increase integration density. A scalable SFQ control system therefore needs a scheme that can address qubits with different transition frequencies using a common clock. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a control scheme for implementing both single- and two-qubit gates. The scheme uses guiding waveforms to rapidly generate bipolar high-speed pulse sequences on a common clock, providing a basis for future implementation in SFQ control systems. Numerically, this scheme achieves a simulated fidelity of 99.99% for 40ns $R(\varphi, \fracπ{2})$ gates with arbitrary initial phases and 99.9% for 100ns controlled-Z(CZ) gates. Experimentally, by utilizing an arbitrary waveform generator(AWG) operated at a fixed sampling rate of 25GSa/s to deliver the bipolar high-speed pulse sequences, we successfully demonstrate 40ns single-qubit gates with an average gate fidelity of 99.94% estimated using cross-entropy benchmarking(XEB) and 120ns CZ gates with 99.63% fidelity. These results demonstrate the feasibility of common-clock encoded pulse control for both single- and two-qubit gates.

papers.title: Learning Similarity-Reduced Ion Kinetics across Scales and Regimes in Capacitively Coupled Plasmas
papers.abstract: Systematic kinetic investigations of discharge-mode and heating-mechanism transitions in low-pressure capacitively coupled plasmas (CCPs) are computationally expensive because particle-in-cell/Monte Carlo collision (PIC/MCC) simulations must resolve the inherently slow ion relaxation. In this Letter, we propose a similarity-reduced ion-kinetic representation and a machine learning (ML) reconstruction method for weakly ionized Boltzmann-Poisson discharge systems. Using discharge similarity, the three-dimensional control parameter space, comprising gas pressure p, gap distance d, and driving frequency f, is reduced into a two-dimensional similarity space (pd, fd). A dual-branch ML model predicts the ion density profile at the reference scale and the conditional ion velocity distribution. Taking a 1D3V argon discharge as the paradigm, we use the reconstructed ion kinetic state to initialize the PIC/MCC simulation, which then relaxes to a self-consistent periodic steady state after only a brief evolution. Compared to conventional uniform initializations, this approach achieves a maximum computational speedup of 56.8 times and a median speedup of 27.7 times. Furthermore, the physical regimes of complex nonlinear discharge transitions, including the alpha-gamma mode transition, local-to-nonlocal electron collisional heating mode transition and low-density jumps, are accurately mapped within the similarity space. Similarity transformations extend these boundaries across scales, opening a new avenue for rapid kinetic characterization and optimization of radio-frequency plasma sources.

papers.title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based pretraining has emerged as a powerful strategy for learning transferable representations in graph neural networks for materials property prediction without requiring quantum-mechanical labels such as energies, forces, and stresses for every pretraining structure. However, the method retains a critical dependency: it requires structures residing near local minima of a potential energy surface, which have traditionally been obtained through costly DFT relaxations of known or physically synthesized compounds. This reliance constrains both the scale and the structural diversity of available pretraining data, leaving large regions of crystal structure space unexplored. In this work, we connect diffusion-based pretraining with synthetic structure generation to reduce this bottleneck. We introduce a synthetic data generation pipeline combining three complementary strategies: perturb-and-relax, generative sampling via MatterGen, and protostructure enumeration. Where structural relaxation is required, we use fast machine-learned interatomic potentials instead of performing a new DFT relaxation for each generated structure. We further compare a coordinate-denoising control with continuous-time variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone. The source comparison covers seven MatBench property-prediction tasks, and an eighth task, \texttt{mp\_gap}, is included in the protostructure scaling study. Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven source-comparison tasks. Scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule numerically matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks; because this protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, the result reflects joint data-and-compute scaling.

papers.title: Perturbative Recovery of Stabilizer-Subspace Correlations for Quantum Computational Chemistry
papers.abstract: Stabilizer-based subspace methods can substantially reduce the quantum resources required for electronic structure calculations, but the resulting projection neglects Hamiltonian couplings to configurations outside the retained subspace. In this work, we introduce Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) to recover the associated correlation contributions, using the Contextual Subspace Variational Quantum Eigensolver (CS-VQE) as a representative application. The central idea is to exploit the Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection as perturbative operators that generate an external manifold from the optimized reference state. Their energetic contributions are evaluated using an Epstein-Nesbet-type second-order correction or a resolvent-based formulation that retains couplings within the external space. By exploiting the factorized structure of the stabilizer-constrained reference state, the required matrix elements can be evaluated through Pauli expectation values on the reduced contextual register without explicitly reconstructing the full-space wave function. Molecular benchmarks demonstrate substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors, allowing chemical precision to be achieved with fewer contextual qubits in several cases. These results establish stabilizer-guided perturbation theory as a promising strategy for improving the accuracy of resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations.

papers.title: QCap: a physics-corrected graph neural network for the capacitance matrix of any planar superconducting device layout
papers.abstract: Electromagnetic simulations of device layouts to extract capacitance are computationally intensive, a major obstacle to accurate design of circuit devices. Machine learning models can bypass these simulations, but previous approaches have been restricted to layouts using only particular components, and require thousands of simulations of those same components as training data. We present QCap, a model that accurately predicts the Maxwell capacitance matrix of an arbitrary superconducting device layout in seconds, compared to minutes to hours of Ansys Q3D simulations. We develop a novel design-embedding algorithm that converts the layout into a universal graph format, allowing the model to work with any layout created with any tool. To achieve high accuracy, we obtain a coarse physics prior from a fast method of moments simulation of capacitance, then train the model to correct this prior. On 4,009 test designs withheld from training data the model outputs agree with Q3D simulations to a median error of 0.177%, and on never-seen component families it stays below 1% error. We demonstrate the model's scaling by obtaining the capacitance matrix of a 9-superconducting-qubit device in 12 seconds on a laptop (compared to 19.9 h and 228 GB of memory in Ansys) with sub-percent error, and capacitance of a (too large to simulate) 100-qubit, 781-conductor device in 3.4 min on a laptop. We provide the open-source models and data on SQuADDS and Hugging Face. Our results provide a powerful tool for large-scale accurate circuit design and guide the development of models to bypass other physical simulations.

papers.title: Structural functional identifiability of unknown differential equation observation maps
papers.abstract: In many differential equation models of real-world systems, the mechanistic structure of the dynamics is known, but the map from the dynamics to the observations is not. This is potentially problematic, as it can prevent us from e.g. learning model parameter values from data. Examples where this occurs include measuring a fluorescent marker as a proxy for the dynamics of a cellular circuit, and using wastewater measurements to follow the development of an epidemic. The nascent field of hybrid modelling, in which machine learning components (like neural networks) are embedded within mechanistic models, provides the tools to learn such maps. Here, the system's dynamics keep their mechanistic form, while a neural network represents the unknown observation map and is trained alongside any unknown core system parameters. This raises a question of identifiability: when can the true observation map be learnt, and when does one simply learn some map that transforms the dynamics into the available data? Building on previous work, we show how structural functional identifiability analysis can establish whether a model's unknown observation maps and core system parameters are identifiable, i.e. can be uniquely learnt from data. We both prove general results on when models with unknown observation maps are, and are not, identifiable, and demonstrate a general methodology (based on differential algebra) for assessing the identifiability of such models. This paves the way for applying classic differential equation workflows to the many real-world systems that contain such unknown maps.

papers.title: Sparse Integer Fourier Transform and Its Application In Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The Discrete Fourier transform, mainly implemented by Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), has been essential for numerous domains, such as digital signal processing and feature extraction in materials design. However, current FFT methods suffer from extensive non-trivial multiplications and twiddle-factor operations in the big data era. To improve the computational efficiency of FFT, this study proposes Sparse Integer Fourier Transform (SIFT), a method that leverages the fast computing of sparsity and small integers, and applies the Radix-n method to derive an FFT. The 2N-point DFT matrix in Radix-n FFT is decomposed into four sparse integer matrices. A diagonal matrix containing complex twiddle factors is efficiently approximated using an optimization strategy while the remaining matrices retain sparsity and integer entries. For radix-32 FFT, SIFT reduces the estimated arithmetic cost by 75%, with RMSE below $2.3765\times10^{-8}$ and MAPE below 0.01089%. We evaluate frequency extraction in a numerical test and an engineering case. In the numerical test, MAPE and RMSE are below 2.016% and $2.536\times10^{-6}$, respectively. For wind turbine fault diagnosis, SIFT extracts compact spectral features that retain fault information while reducing the classifier's input dimensionality relative to the full time series.

papers.title: Probing the real-time decoding accuracy bounds in trapped ion architectures
papers.abstract: Fault tolerant quantum computers will rely on real-time decoders that process syndromes faster than the QEC cycle duration. The millisecond cycle times offered by trapped ion platforms relax low-latency decoding demands, but simulations and experiments have not yet exploited this time budget to reach maximum logical error suppression.
